p.s: In 2026, it will be the 50th Anniversary of the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (SSRL) SR and protein crystallography initiative led by Keith Hodgson and published in 1976.

This seminal research led to an explosion of experimental protein crystal structures these past 5 decades whereby 90% of protein crystal structures are determined at synchrotron X-radiation facilities.
It is the vast number of structures now totalling 240,000 in the Protein Data Bank that underpinned the AlphaFold prediction of protein folds.
In 2026, it will be the 50th Anniversary of the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (SSRL) SR and protein crystallography initiative led by Keith Hodgson and published in 1976 in PNAS [1].

Recognizing this the IUCr's Journal of Synchrotron Radiation (JSR) produced a special issue entitled 'The 50th Anniversary of the Stanford SSRL SR and protein crystallography initiative led by Keith Hodgson'.
The majority of the world's SR and XFEL facilities submitted articles for this in JSR.
This collection of articles is introduced by Helliwell and Szebenyi [2] here: https://journals.iucr.org/special_issues/2025/ssrlprotein/.

This seminal research by Keith Hodgson led to an explosion of experimental protein crystal structures these past 5 decades whereby 90% of protein crystal structures are determined at synchrotron X-radiation facilities.

The first reference of ref. [1] was to a paper from the DESY Synchrotron Laboratory in Hamburg, Germany [3] focussing on the broader range of the whole of biological diffraction and the great potential of synchrotron radiation.
Indeed, in parallel with the paper from SSRL [1] was the paper from DESY, Hamburg [4].
All three of these papers were important.
These vital steps included the multiple wavelength phasing method with SR, which is fully tuneable, led by Keith Hodgson and documented in refs.
Those papers cited the two-wavelength phasing for an iron containing protein with two laboratory X-ray sources, one with a Ni anode and one with a Co anode [9].
These stimulated my practical activity in this field [10].

The much more versatile synchrotron radiation method was expanded in its applicability in a major way by the seleno-methionine protein production methodology initiated by Wayne Hendrickson [11] who also expanded the multiple wavelength phasing method, 'MAD' [12,13].

Helliwell, initially in Keele, then York and Manchester Universities, and as a beamline scientist at the UK's SRS established protein crystallography beamlines (7.2, 9.6 and 9.5) between 1979 and 2008.
These also made sustained and broad contributions to this vital protein crystal structure determining method.
A key issue was considering how many X-ray wavelengths were necessary for a precise determination of the phases of the X-ray reflections.

It had been established by Hoppe and Jakubowski [9] what was needed in principle and indeed in practice with their home laboratory X-ray sources applied in their actual case of erythrocruorin that two wavelengths were sufficient leading to a dispersive difference and one anomalous difference, three measurements in all.
Helliwell's laboratory explored the number of wavelengths in various combinations up to four and their dispersive and anomalous differences measurements needs in detail [14] using SRS 9.5.
For new protein crystal structures, at SSRL Keith Hodgson led the research on the copper containing cucumber basic protein, which was amongst the first [15] and a critical demonstration of MAD.
The French LURE synchrotron facility [16] also made important demonstration studies as did the NSLS and elsewhere [12,13].
Mukherjee, Helliwell and Main [17] combined direct methods with SR anomalous differences data measured at the SRS 7.2.
This innovation allowed the positions of the anomalous scatterers in a protein to be done using the direct methods program MULTAN [18].
This was a critical step as the cases increased where larger numbers of anomalous scatterers were harnessed in the MAD phase determinations.
For locating relatively large numbers of anomalous scatterers efficiently from MAD or SAD data SHELXD was developed [19].
SHELXD's approach involved iterative dual-space direct methods, i.e. based on phase refinement in reciprocal space and peak picking in real space.
The planning of the ESRF's macromolecular crystallography in the mid-1980s and into the 1990s [20] created a great expansion of synchrotron radiation usage in protein crystallography.
Greatly facilitating the detailing of these plans was the 'New Rings Workshop' held at SSRL, co-organized by Keith Hodgson with Dr Herman Winick, a Stanford accelerator machine physicist.
Critical were the tests on protein microcrystals showing that a 20-micron dimension microcrystal could withstand the radiation and thermal blast of such ultra-intense X-ray beams [21].
One of the first MAD experiments done at ESRF was on BM14 [22].
The eventual extensive development of instrumentation and methods for multi-wavelength anomalous dispersion worldwide namely at the SRS, ESRF, CHESS and Elettra facilities was described in [23].

Keith Hodgson's experience in SR EXAFS on a wide range of bioinorganic chemistry samples enabled the synergy between tuneable X-ray synchrotron radiation for multiple wavelength phasing in crystallography and scanning of the X-ray wavelength in measuring EXAFS spectra put him in a pivotal position to develop both scientific fields.
The International Union of Crystallography (IUCr) established a Commission on XAFS in 1996 (http://ww1.iucr.org/iucr-top/cexec/rep96/cxafs.htm).

Improved X-ray detectors over the commonly used photographic film in the 1970s for measuring small intensity signals was another critical component of the ultimate success of the MAD phasing method and macromolecular crystallography in general (see relevant sections in refs [24][25][26]).
At SSRL led by Keith Hodgson their multi-wire proportional chamber (MWPC) was a critical step and was used in their determination of the crystal structure of the cucumber basic protein [15].
At LURE, Fourme and Kahn adapted George Charpak's CERN radial drift chamber MWPC for multiple wavelength phasing.

SRS collaborated with Enraf Nonius commercializing the Arndt (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge) TV intensifier detector, with Rigaku Corporation Japan with their image plage detector reader and the UK Rutherford Appleton Laboratory with a multiwire proportional chamber.
See chapter 5 of ref. [24].

These improved detectors each had their strengths and limitations and became superseded by the ideal properties pixel detector developed at the Swiss PSI Laboratory and commercialized by their spin out company Dectris [27].
Software developed for multiple isomorphous replacement was harnessed for multiple wavelength phasing, such as in the MLPHARE program of CCP4 [28].
Eventually, as the diffraction intensity measurements became better quality (i.e.

lower errors) due to the improved detectors, single wavelength phasing became routine where the ambiguity in each reflection phase from its one anomalous difference was resolved by solvent flattening, a procedure led by Wang [29].
There were some false steps, and temporary challenges, in developing the MAD phasing method.

These included: the need for at least four wavelengths for a least squares analysis of phases which were unnecessary (as shown by [14]); the proposal of Arndt to make a polychromatic profile, made feasible in experimental terms by SRS 7.2 [30] although that did become applied in inorganic small molecule crystallography as the renamed method of DAFS (diffraction anomalous fine structure) was called [31].

An important experimental approach initially, when the synchrotron source X-ray beam intensity could vary with time, was a well aligned protein crystal to ensure the anomalous differences were measured at the same time to improve their precision as much as possible [32,33].
There are some key developments need mentioning to offer a more rounded narrative of the story.
For instance, with the advent of third generation light sources as mentioned above specialized micro focusing diffractometers became available, with seminal work done at ESRF [34].
This allowed to routinely significantly reduce the sample size.
Soft X-ray phasing became available, and it involved new beamline and software developments (see review [35]).
Multibend achromat devices in the machine accelerators themselves have become available in the last 15 years promising brilliance never expected before [36].
Several Nobel prizes have been awarded in structural biology where synchrotron radiation protein crystallography played a key role.
AlphaFold [37] is now dominating macromolecular crystal structure determination as the start for molecular replacement [38].
Indeed it is the vast number of structures now totalling 240,000 in the Protein Data Bank that underpinned the AlphaFold prediction of protein folds.
Optimized anomalous differences using a variable X-ray wavelength continue to have a strong role to play in macromolecular crystallography.
About a third of all proteins are metalloproteins.
So, to be certain of the type of metal and the metal atom locations is done using a tuneable synchrotron radiation beamline.

Furthermore, all the domains of macromolecular X-ray crystallography were changed by the breakthrough led by Keith Hodgson at SSRL in 1976 whereby 90% of protein crystal structures are determined at synchrotron X-radiation facilities.

We are seeing several other developments in synchrotron radiation macromolecular crystallography besides structure determination and ensuring precision of metal atom identification and location just mentioned.
First, beamline facilities for studies of time-resolved changes in structure is a major focus to help elucidate functional mechanisms (see the recent book by Moffat and Lattman [39]).
Second, searching for new binding fragments in the search for new drugs has led to dedicated beamlines for these activities (for a recent overview from an industry perspective, see [40]).

An effort is underway to investigate macromolecular crystal structures determined at 'body temperatures' such as 37°C for patient relevance and at thermophile and hyperthermophile organisms' temperatures [41].

Third the democratization of science that centralized beamlines have brought has put the synchrotron facilities in a pivotal position to similarly administer centralized electron cryomicroscopy facilities.
These can also include instruments for neutron macromolecular crystallography; the Photon and Neutrons Campus in Grenoble also with cryoEM is one such with multiprobe centres [42].
Taken altogether these facilities, and allied methods, have brought great opportunities for the structural biologist and structural chemist.
A recent book describing all these is [26].
No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author.
